title: The Wolf and the Lion
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A wolf stole a lamb from the flock, and was carrying it off to devour it at his leisure when he met a Lion, who took his prey away from him and walked off with it. He dared not resist, but when the Lion had gone some distance he said, "It is most unjust of you to take what's mine away from me like that." The Lion laughed and called out in reply, "It was justly yours, no doubt! The gift of a friend, perhaps, eh?"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Wolf steal from the flock?
options: A lamb
A goat
A calf
A ram

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whom did the Wolf meet while carrying off the lamb?
options: A Lion
A shepherd
Another wolf
A hunting dog

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Lion do upon meeting the Wolf?
options: He warned the Wolf to release the lamb
He took the prey away and walked off with it
He ignored the Wolf and continued on his way
He asked the Wolf to share the lamb

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the Wolf not fight back when the Lion took the lamb?
options: He dared not resist
He was too injured to fight
He decided the lamb was not worth it
He was distracted by another animal

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Wolf call the Lion's action once the Lion has gone some distance?
options: A wise decision
Most unjust
Perfectly fair
A generous gift

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Lion respond to the Wolf's complaint?
options: He apologizes and returns the lamb
He laughs and suggests the lamb was itself a stolen gift
He threatens to attack the Wolf
He offers the Wolf a share of the meat

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "leisure" mean in "devour it at his leisure"?
options: In great haste
At an unhurried, comfortable pace
In secret, without being seen
With great difficulty

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the Lion's reply to the Wolf ironic?
options: It points out that the Wolf's own claim to the lamb was no more just than the Lion's taking of it
It reveals the Lion actually agrees the Wolf was treated unfairly
It shows the Lion did not realize the lamb had been stolen
It proves the Lion intends to return the lamb after all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what exact words does the Wolf use to complain to the Lion?
options: "You will pay for this someday"
"It is most unjust of you to take what's mine away from me like that"
"Give me back my lamb at once"
"I will tell the shepherd what you did"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what exact words does the Lion use in his reply?
options: "Consider it a lesson well learned"
"It was justly yours, no doubt! The gift of a friend, perhaps, eh?"
"I take what I please, and you know it"
"Next time, run faster"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, from where did the Wolf originally steal the lamb?
options: From the flock
From a farmer's yard
From another wolf's den
From a market stall

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "unjust" mean in "It is most unjust of you"?
options: Unfair
Unwise
Unexpected
Unfriendly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Lion's mention of "the gift of a friend" suggest about how he views the Wolf's claim to the lamb?
options: He believes the Wolf's ownership of the lamb was just as illegitimate as his own taking of it
He genuinely believes a friend gave the Wolf the lamb
He thinks the Wolf earned the lamb fairly through hard work
He plans to ask the Wolf who the friend was

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Lion seizes a lamb the Wolf had stolen, and mocks the Wolf's complaint by pointing out the lamb was never rightfully his either
A Wolf and a Lion share a stolen lamb peacefully
A Lion returns a stolen lamb to its rightful shepherd
A Wolf outsmarts a Lion and keeps the lamb for himself
